parts.title: Frog vs Mosquito: SAME or DIFFERENT? Count the Stages! (Part 1) | How to Compare Life Cycles
parts.description:
A frog and a mosquito both lay their eggs in water, and both have young that look nothing like the adult. So are their life cycles the same? Lock in your answer from last time, find out how to compare two life cycles properly, be a raindrop and count the stages in a pond and a flower-pot plate, and spot Pip's mistake about the frog and the grasshopper. Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Life Cycles of Animals.

In this part:
• Frog and mosquito: the same life cycle? (last episode's dare)
• Look closer: what is the same, and what is different
• Be a raindrop: count the stages (three for the frog, four for the mosquito)
• Observable characteristics: what we can see and count
• HOLD ON! Are the frog and the grasshopper exactly the same?
• Look closer: the young beside their parents
• Spot the hidden cicada!

Key words: similarities, differences, observable characteristics.
Watch Part 2: which came first, the chicken or the egg? Last episode: the caterpillar that becomes a butterfly, and the mosquito's life cycle.

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies!

Frog vs mosquito: same or different? P3 Science, Chapter 5, Life Cycles of Animals (pp. 90 to 98): how to compare two life cycles (similarities and differences, by observable characteristics: the number of stages and the physical features), why a life cycle has no first or last stage, and why life cycles matter. This episode closes the Cycles theme. Also fits US NGSS 3-LS1-1 (Grade 3: life cycles).
Safety and care: We watch hens from a distance. We look at bees and cicadas and do not touch them. Class mealworms are kept with food and air holes and go back to class. Tip out still water so mosquitoes cannot breed.
Try it at home: Pick two animals from the last three episodes and tell someone at home one thing that is the same about their life cycles and one thing that is different.
Some schools and parks in Singapore plant butterfly gardens, with the plants butterflies lay their eggs on, like lime plants for the lime butterfly. More plants, more eggs, more butterflies.
In the US, Grade 3 classes plant milkweed so monarch butterflies have somewhere to lay their eggs.
The Cycles theme: C1. What makes up a cycle? A repeated pattern of change. C2. How does a cycle help us predict events and processes? We know what comes next. C3. Why are cycles important to life? Life cycles ensure that living things of the same kind can continue to live on Earth.

parts.title: Which Came First, the Chicken or the EGG? (Part 2) | No First or Last Stage, Why Life Cycles Matter
parts.description:
The hen is sitting on her eggs. So which came first, the chicken or the egg? Lock in your answer, be an egg and go all the way round, put your finger anywhere on the loop, spot the mistake in Momo's homework on the mosquito and the mealworm beetle, and find out why life cycles matter. Part 2 of Primary 3 Science, Life Cycles of Animals.

In this part:
• Which came first, the chicken or the egg?
• Be an egg: egg, chick, hen, and round again
• Look closer: a loop has no first or last stage (like day and night)
• Showdown: find the mistake in Momo's homework (the mosquito and the mealworm beetle)
• Look closer: same stages, still different (physical features)
• Why life cycles matter: the butterfly lays an egg
• A chant to remember it all
• Spot the hidden honeybee!

Key words: repeated, no first or last stage, physical features.
Watch Part 1 first! Next episode: a magnet, a steel pin and a copper wire. Which one will the magnet pull?
